As of 350 PM EST Tuesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Cool and dry tonight, becoming mostly cloudy on
Wednesday, with rain chances increasing from S to N during the 
day. 

The latest WX analysis shows strong (>1035mb) sfc high pressure
centered across the Great Lakes, riding into the local area, with
a trough of low pressure off the east coast of Florida to the 
Bahamas. Dry and mainly clear skies prevail along and W of I-95,
with high clouds closer to the coast. Breezy N-NE winds continue
to the E of I-95, with diminishing winds to the west. 
Temperatures are primarily in the lower 50s this afternoon with 
dew pts in the 20s and 30s. As the sfc high builds eastward this
evening, winds drop off inland, but stay elevated near the 
coast. Lows range from around 30 degrees in the piedmont to the 
low/mid 30s near I-95 and upper 30s and low 40s closer to the 
coast. Clouds increase after midnight so expect temperatures to
drop off fast this evening, then becoming nearly steady 
overnight. Mostly cloudy Wednesday, with rain chances increasing
from S to N during the late morning/early afternoon hours. 
Rainfall amounts through 00Z/Thursday (7PM Wed) will be fairly 
light except across far southern VA/ NE NC. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...High confidence for an impactful storm across 
the region Wednesday night into Thanksgiving Day with strong 
winds and moderate to heavy rainfall expected.

The aforementioned surface high will continue to build/migrate 
eastward into New England Wednesday night, strengthening to 
1040+mb. Models show a distinct CAD pressure pattern as high 
pressure ridges southward to the east of the higher terrain. Low
pressure develops off the Southeast coast in response to 
several short wave troughs in both the northern and southern 
stream jets. 12z guidance continues to struggle to resolve 
exactly how this interaction will play out with some remaining 
uncertainty in the details of surface low track and strength
(12z Euro still more phased than the GFS). Regardless, with 
very strong high pressure to the north a near certainty, the 
pressure gradient will steepen dramatically to bring a very 
impactful storm system across the area Wednesday night into the 
Thanksgiving holiday. Low pressure will develop off the SC coast
Wednesday afternoon and lift northward overnight. Strong easterly
winds to the north of the deepening low will bring copious 
Atlantic moisture into the region with PoPs rapidly increasing 
from S to N late Wednesday afternoon through the evening. 
Periods of moderate to locally heavy rainfall will spread 
northward overnight into Thanksgiving. 12z ensemble and 
deterministic guidance now shows widespread 2-3" storm total QPF
with southeastern portions of the area potentially averaging 
3-4". While this will be beneficial rainfall, a lot of this 
precip is forecast to fall in a relatively short period of time 
and could lead to areas of flash flooding. WPC has upgraded to a
Slight Risk (level 2/4) across SE portions of the area through 
7 AM Thursday with the entire region in Marginal Risk thereafter.
In addition to the heavy rain potential, strong winds will also
be of concern, especially near the coast. The latest forecast 
shows wind gusts 30-40 mph for areas along and west of I-95 and 
35-45 mph gusts to 50+ mph possible to the east. For areas 
along the coast and near the Chesapeake Bay, wind gusts of 50-60
mph are possible. A High Wind Watch has been expanded to VA
Beach/Norfolk/ NC OBX in addition to the entire Eastern Shore 
where confidence in seeing a period of 50-60 mph gusts is 
highest. Wind Advisories are increasingly likely for at least 
the eastern half of the area in subsequent forecasts as details 
regarding the exact strength and track of surface low pressure 
resolve. The surface low lifts north of the area by Thursday 
evening with rain ending from S to N. Winds become SW and 
decrease somewhat as the low passes by. It will remain breezy 
overnight with gusty SW winds becoming W/SW into Friday 
afternoon. With many folks likely to be traveling during the 
peak impacts from this system, users should closely monitor the 
forecast over the next 24 hours as specific details on low track
and strength come into focus. 


KEY MESSAGE 3...Widespread moderate to major coastal flooding is 
expected Thursday into Friday, with the greatest threat likely 
during the Thanksgiving morning high tide for most locations. 

Confidence has increased further this cycle regarding a very significant
coastal flooding event as strong and prolonged onshore winds 
associated with a developing low pressure system coincide with 
elevated astronomical tides. The ongoing King Tide cycle, full 
moon, and lunar perigee will result in unusually high astronomical
tides, increasing the potential for substantial coastal flooding
as tidal departures rise ahead of the approaching system. 
Latest guidance continues to depict a strong area of high 
pressure over New England, with low pressure tracking N to N
